blocks.content: The history of Andhra Pradesh spans several millennia and encompasses some of the most significant dynasties, empires, and cultural movements on the Indian subcontinent. The region was inhabited since prehistoric times, and ancient texts such as the Aitareya Brahmana mention the Andhras as a distinct people.
2.1 Ancient Period
2.1.1 Prehistoric and Early History

Archaeological excavations at sites such as Kurnool Caves (Billasurgam), Nagarjunakonda, and Amaravati have revealed evidence of human habitation dating back to the Stone Age. The Kurnool Caves contain paintings and artifacts belonging to the Mesolithic and Neolithic periods. The region is mentioned in the Aitareya Brahmana (circa 800 BCE) as the land of the Andhras.

Andhra rulers are mentioned in Ashoka's edicts (circa 250 BCE) as recipients of Buddhist teachings. The Mauryan Empire under Chandragupta Maurya and later Ashoka extended its influence over the northern parts of the Andhra region. After the decline of the Mauryas, indigenous dynasties rose to prominence.
2.1.2 Satavahana Dynasty (230 BCE – 220 CE)

The Satavahanas, also known as Andhras, were one of the earliest and most powerful dynasties of the Deccan. They established a vast empire stretching from the Vindhyas in the north to the Krishna River in the south. Their capital was initially at Pratishthana (modern Paithan in Maharashtra) and later shifted to Amaravati and Dhanyakataka. The Satavahanas played a crucial role in trade between India and the Roman Empire, and they were great patrons of Buddhism, constructing numerous stupas and monasteries.

The most prominent Satavahana ruler was Gautamiputra Satakarni (78–102 CE), who defeated the Shakas, Pahlavas, and Yavanas, and consolidated the Satavahana power. He is described in inscriptions as 'the destroyer of the pride of the Kshatriyas.' The Satavahanas issued bilingual (Prakrit and Brahmi) coins and inscriptions, and promoted Prakrit as a court language.
2.1.3 Ikshvaku Dynasty (225–340 CE)

After the decline of the Satavahanas, the Ikshvaku dynasty rose to power in the Krishna-Guntur region. Their capital was at Vijayapuri (Nagarjunakonda). The Ikshvakus were great patrons of Buddhism, and under their rule, Nagarjunakonda became an important Buddhist center attracting monks from Sri Lanka, China, and Central Asia. Nagarjuna, the great Buddhist philosopher, is believed to have lived during this period.
2.1.4 Pallava Dynasty (275–897 CE)

The Pallavas originally ruled the region around Kanchipuram (in modern Tamil Nadu) but exercised significant influence over southern Andhra Pradesh. They were great builders and patrons of art and architecture, with the rock-cut temples of Mahabalipuram being their most famous contribution. The Pallavas had prolonged conflicts with the Chalukyas of Badami and the Rashtrakutas.
2.2 Medieval Period
2.2.1 Eastern Chalukyas of Vengi (624–1189 CE)

The Eastern Chalukyas ruled from Vengi (near modern Eluru) and were a branch of the Chalukyas of Badami. Their long reign of over 500 years was a period of significant cultural and literary development for the Telugu people. Under their patronage, Telugu literature flourished, and the Nannaya, the first Telugu poet who translated the Mahabharata into Telugu, worked during this period (circa 1022 CE).
2.2.2 Rashtrakutas (753–982 CE)

The Rashtrakutas dominated parts of the Deccan including Andhra Pradesh for over two centuries. They were great patrons of Jainism and commissioned notable artistic works such as the Kailasa Temple at Ellora. Their conflicts with the Eastern Chalukyas, Pallavas, and Gurjara-Pratiharas shaped medieval Deccan politics.
2.2.3 Western Chalukyas of Kalyani (973–1198 CE)

The Western Chalukyas of Kalyani, also known as the Kalyani Chalukyas or Later Chalukyas, dominated large parts of the Deccan after defeating the Rashtrakutas. They exercised suzerainty over parts of Andhra Pradesh. The period saw continued development of Telugu literature and temple architecture. The Tailapa II who founded this branch was a feudatory of the Rashtrakutas.
2.2.4 Kakatiya Dynasty (1083–1323 CE)

The Kakatiyas were one of the most important Telugu dynasties. They established their capital at Warangal (Orugallu) and ruled over most of present-day Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. The Kakatiyas were great builders and administrators. Prataparudra I and Prataparudra II were their most renowned rulers. The Warangal Fort, the Thousand Pillared Temple at Hanamkonda, and the Ramappa Temple (UNESCO World Heritage Site) are their architectural masterpieces.

Rudramadevi (circa 1262–1289 CE) was a remarkable queen of the Kakatiya dynasty who ruled in her own right, one of the few women rulers of medieval India. The Kakatiya kingdom fell to the Delhi Sultanate under Malik Kafur in 1310 and later finally conquered by Muhammad bin Tughluq in 1323.
2.2.5 Reddy Kingdoms (1325–1448 CE)

After the fall of the Kakatiyas, the Reddy chieftains established independent kingdoms in coastal Andhra. The Kondaveedu Reddys and the Rajahmundry Reddys were the two main branches. Prolaya Vema Reddy and Anavema Reddy were notable rulers. The period saw significant contributions to Telugu literature, with the Ashtadiggajas (Eight Great Poets) being patronized by the Vijayanagara rulers who later absorbed the Reddy kingdoms.
2.2.6 Vijayanagara Empire (1336–1646 CE)

The Vijayanagara Empire, founded by Harihara I and Bukka Raya I in 1336, became one of the greatest empires in Indian history. Although their capital Hampi is in present-day Karnataka, the empire included all of Andhra Pradesh. The Vijayanagara rulers were great patrons of Telugu literature, art, and architecture.

The most glorious period was under Krishnadevaraya (1509–1529 CE), who was himself a distinguished Telugu poet (Amuktamalyada) and patron of the Ashtadiggajas. He defeated the Bijapur Sultanate and the Orissa Gajapatis. The Battle of Talikota (1565 CE) between the Vijayanagara Empire and the Deccan Sultanates (Bidar, Bijapur, Ahmadnagar, and Golconda) led to the sack of Hampi and the gradual decline of the empire.
2.2.7 Qutb Shahi Dynasty of Golconda (1512–1687 CE)

The Golconda Sultanate was one of the Deccan Sultanates that emerged after the breakup of the Bahmani Sultanate. The Qutb Shahis ruled from Golconda (near Hyderabad) and extended their control over large parts of Andhra. Golconda became famous for its diamond mines, producing legendary gems like the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope Diamond. The Qutb Shahis patronized art, architecture, and poetry, and the Golconda Fort and the Charminar (built by Muhammad Quli Qutb Shah in 1591) are their architectural legacies. The Golconda Sultanate was finally annexed by the Mughal Emperor Aurangzeb in 1687.
2.3 Modern Period
2.3.1 Nizam of Hyderabad (1724–1948)

After the Mughal decline, Mir Qamar-ud-Din Khan (Nizam-ul-Mulk Asaf Jah I) established the Hyderabad State in 1724. The Nizams of Hyderabad ruled a vast territory that included most of present-day Telangana, parts of Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, and Karnataka. Hyderabad was one of the wealthiest princely states and one of the largest in British India. The last Nizam, Mir Osman Ali Khan (1911–1948), was once considered the richest man in the world.

After India's independence in 1947, the Nizam attempted to maintain independence or seek accession to Pakistan. However, the Indian government launched Operation Polo (also called the Police Action) in September 1948, under the command of General J.N. Chaudhuri and under the political leadership of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel, which resulted in the annexation of Hyderabad into the Indian Union.
2.3.2 British Rule in Andhra

The coastal districts of Andhra came under British East India Company control in stages. The Northern Circars were ceded by the Nizam to the British in 1766. Madras Presidency (later Madras Province) administered coastal Andhra for most of the British period. The region witnessed several uprisings including the Vizianagaram Rebellion (1794), Tribal Uprisings in the Agency area, and participation in the 1857 revolt.

The national movement in Andhra was strongly influenced by leaders like Potti Sriramulu, who fasted unto death demanding a separate Telugu-speaking state. His death on 15 December 1952 triggered massive protests that compelled the Indian government to create Andhra State on 1 October 1953, becoming the first state in India to be formed on a linguistic basis.
2.3.3 Formation of Andhra State and Andhra Pradesh

Andhra State was created on 1 October 1953 by separating the Telugu-speaking areas from Madras State. Kurnool was its first capital, and T. Prakasam became its first Chief Minister. Subsequently, the States Reorganisation Act of 1956 led to the merger of Andhra State with the Telugu-speaking regions of Hyderabad State (then part of Hyderabad State administered separately from Indian Union) to form Andhra Pradesh on 1 November 1956, with Hyderabad as its capital.
2.3.4 Bifurcation and Formation of Telangana (2014)

The Telangana movement, demanding a separate state for the Telangana region (comprising 10 districts), gained momentum over several decades. The Andhra Pradesh Reorganisation Act, 2014 was passed by the Indian Parliament, and on 2 June 2014, the new state of Telangana was carved out. The residual Andhra Pradesh comprised 13 districts with a predominantly coastal and Rayalaseema geography. Hyderabad was made the joint capital for a transitional period of up to 10 years.
